body_markdown:
Florida health officials are warning residents to take mosquito-borne illnesses seriously as the state continues to record locally acquired cases of dengue fever. Health surveillance data indicate that dengue transmission is occurring within Florida communities, raising concerns that the number of cases could increase as mosquito activity continues.


Dengue is a viral infection transmitted primarily through the bite of infected mosquitoes. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the illness can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and rash. While many people recover, dengue can sometimes become severe and potentially life-threatening.


## Florida Reports Locally Acquired Dengue Cases


Florida's arbovirus surveillance data showed that, as of the period leading up to September 1, 2026, the state had reported 73 locally acquired dengue cases and 14 mosquito pools across five counties.


The term "locally acquired" is important because it means the infection was contracted within Florida rather than during international travel. Local transmission suggests that infected mosquitoes are present in the community and can potentially spread the virus to additional people.


The Florida Department of Health continues to monitor mosquito activity and human cases as part of its broader surveillance and disease prevention efforts.


The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) has also urged residents to take preventive measures. Peter Jiang, PhD, president of the FMCA, emphasized that mosquito control serves an important public health function beyond simply reducing mosquito bites.


For Florida residents, the message is straightforward: reducing mosquito exposure can help lower the risk of contracting diseases carried by these insects.


## Why Dengue Is Sometimes Called "Break-Bone Fever"


Dengue can produce symptoms that range from mild to severe. One of its most recognizable characteristics is intense pain affecting the muscles, joints and bones.


Because of the severity of this pain, dengue is sometimes referred to as "break-bone fever."


Other symptoms can include high fever, headache, nausea, vomiting and a skin rash. Some people infected with dengue may experience few or no symptoms, while others can become seriously ill.


Severe dengue may lead to complications such as bleeding, shock or organ impairment. Anyone experiencing concerning symptoms, particularly after being exposed to mosquitoes in an area where dengue is circulating, should seek medical advice.


Residents should not assume that every mosquito bite will result in illness. However, ongoing local transmission makes mosquito bite prevention an important part of protecting individual and community health.


## Tampa Bay Area Sees Local Transmission


The Tampa Bay area has been an important focus of dengue surveillance in Florida. The FMCA has reported more than 30 human cases of locally acquired dengue in the Tampa Bay region.


Hillsborough County has also reported locally acquired dengue infections. Following confirmation of an eighth human case in the county, the Hillsborough County Department of Health issued a mosquito-borne illness alert.


Health authorities are continuing surveillance and mosquito control efforts in affected communities.


These measures are particularly important because mosquitoes can transmit several different viruses and parasites. The American Mosquito Control Association notes that mosquitoes can serve as vectors for diseases including dengue, West Nile virus, yellow fever, Zika virus, malaria and chikungunya.


## How Florida Residents Can Reduce Mosquito Bites


Health officials recommend several practical steps to reduce exposure to mosquitoes.


One of the simplest precautions is to wear clothing that limits exposed skin. Loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants can provide an additional physical barrier against mosquito bites.


Residents can also use insect repellents registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Repellents should be applied according to the instructions on their labels.


Homes should also be checked for places where mosquitoes can enter. Damaged screens on windows, doors, porches and patios should be repaired when possible.


Another important step is eliminating standing water.


Mosquitoes can lay eggs in relatively small amounts of stagnant water. Containers around homes and yards can therefore become potential breeding sites. Residents should regularly empty water from items such as discarded tires, buckets, pool covers, coolers, toys and flowerpots.


Water that accumulates after rainfall or lawn sprinkling should not be allowed to remain unnecessarily.


## West Nile Virus Cases Also Rising


Dengue is not the only mosquito-borne disease being monitored in the United States.


West Nile virus (WNV) has also been reported in several states during 2026. New York City health officials recently announced a locally identified WNV infection involving a resident who had spent time outdoors and in locations outside the city.


CDC surveillance data showed eight human West Nile virus cases reported in New York state during 2026 as of the information cited in the report.


Nationwide, reported human WNV cases increased substantially during the summer. CDC data showed 407 cases as of September 8, compared with 32 cases recorded in July.


Arizona had the highest number of reported cases at 88, followed by California with 66 and Texas with 46.


Health officials have stressed that mosquito season remains active and that people should take precautions to avoid bites.


## Mosquito Prevention Remains Important


The increasing number of mosquito-borne disease reports serves as a reminder that prevention is not limited to one particular virus.


A single mosquito bite does not necessarily lead to infection, but avoiding bites can reduce the potential risk of exposure to several diseases. Removing standing water, using appropriate insect repellent, wearing protective clothing and maintaining window and door screens are relatively simple measures that can make a difference.


Florida's warm climate provides conditions in which mosquitoes can remain active for extended periods. Continued surveillance therefore remains important for identifying areas where mosquito-borne diseases may be circulating.


Residents should also pay attention to public health alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health and local county health departments.


As locally acquired dengue cases continue to be reported, health officials are encouraging Floridians to remain vigilant rather than wait until mosquito-borne illnesses become more widespread.


## What Residents Should Remember


Florida's reported locally acquired dengue cases demonstrate that dengue transmission can occur within U.S. communities, even when an individual has not recently traveled internationally.


The most effective approach is prevention. Residents can reduce potential exposure by avoiding mosquito bites and eliminating standing water around their homes.


Anyone who develops symptoms consistent with dengue or another mosquito-borne infection should contact a healthcare professional, especially if they have recently been in an area where transmission has been reported.


Mosquito control is ultimately a community effort. Individual precautions, local surveillance and public mosquito-control programs can work together to reduce the risk of disease transmission.
